xref.title: Inspiration for Band-Aid (November 11, 1984)
xref.body: On the evening of November 11, 1984, after a difficult day attempting to publicize The Boomtown Rats' album "In the Long Grass," Bob Geldof watched a BBC documentary by reporter Michael Buerk detailing the famine in Ethiopia. Deeply affected by the images of starvation, Geldof felt compelled to take action, leading to the inception of the Band-Aid project. "Bob was stunned by the images of starving people, and he was suddenly moved to do something, anything to help these poor people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

xref.title: Recording "Do They Know It's Christmas?" (November 25, 1984)
xref.body: Just two weeks after Bob Geldof saw the BBC documentary on the Ethiopian famine, 25 of Britain's most renowned musicians assembled at Sarm Studios in London's Notting Hill area on November 25, 1984. They gathered to record the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?", which marked the official beginning of the Band-Aid project. "On November the 25th, 1984, just two weeks after that BBC broadcast, 25 of Britain's most famous musicians gathered at Sarm studios in the Notting Hill area of London to crank out a song that was now called Do They Know It's Christmas?"

xref.title: First Meeting with Paula Yates (1985)
xref.body: As a guest on the British TV show *The Tube* in 1985, he met host Paula Yates, then partnered with Bob Geldof. He immediately asked her to return to his hotel room; she declined, but a strong connection was established, potentially initiating an affair. "In 1985, Hutchins was a guest on the British TV show The Tube. The host was Paula Yates, and she, for the last 10 years, had been with Bob Geldoff, he of the Bumpton Rats and the organizer of Live Aid."

xref.title: SNL Pope John Paul II Photo Tear (October 3, 1992) – Career-Ending Television Moment
xref.body: After a series of controversies (refusing to appear on SNL while Andrew Dice Clay was host in 1990; refusing the national anthem before a New Jersey show in August 1990; skipping the 1991 Grammys despite four nominations; a perceived pro-Saddam comment in March 1991), Sinead O'Connor appeared on *Saturday Night Live* on October 3, 1992, singing Bob Marley's "War." In rehearsal she held a picture of a refugee child; live, she substituted a photo of Pope John Paul II — taken from her mother's bedroom wall — and tore it up at the word "evil," saying "fight the real enemy." There was complete silence from the studio audience. NBC received nearly 5,000 complaints and the resulting media blowback permanently ended her mainstream career. The inspiration was Bob Geldof tearing up a picture of John Travolta on *Top of the Pops* in the 1970s. "NBC received almost 5,000 complaints. The blowback in the media was intense and her career never, ever recovered."

xref.title: Live 8 Reunion (2005)
xref.body: Pink Floyd reunited for a performance at the Live 8 concert on July 2nd, 2005, which was considered one of the biggest attractions of the global benefit event. This reunion was notably engineered by Bob Geldof, highlighting the significant draw of the band. "And one of the biggest attractions was a reunion of Pink Floyd, only something that Bob Geldoff could have engineered."

xref.title: Bob Geldof's Self-Perception and Motivation
xref.body: As described in his autobiography, Bob Geldof felt his limited influence as a "not very successful pop singer" making records "that no one bought" underscored his initial dilemma in responding to the Ethiopian famine. This self-assessment, however, fueled his determination to find a way to make a difference, ultimately leading to the creation of Band-Aid. "As he wrote in his autobiography, I was only a pop singer, and by now not a very successful pop singer, all I could do was make records that no one bought."

xref.title: Fatherhood and Custody Strain
xref.body: He became a father to Heavenly Hiraani Tiger Lily with Paula Yates. Despite his pride in fatherhood, he was caught in the midst of the contentious custody battle between Yates and Bob Geldof, a strain that worsened his addictions and existing predilections. "Michael and Paula were the parents of a baby girl named Heveli, Herani, Tiger Lily. And while he was proud to be a father, Michael was caught in the middle of everything between Paula and Bob."

xref.title: Initial Idea for a Benefit Record
xref.body: The day after being deeply affected by the BBC documentary on the Ethiopian famine, Bob Geldof tentatively proposed the idea of a benefit record for Ethiopia at his record company's office. The suggestion was well-received by those present, setting the stage for the Band-Aid project. "he tentatively suggested that someone ought to put out a record for the Ethiopians. A benefit thing."

xref.title: Last Call with Bob Geldof
xref.body: Between 4 AM and 5 AM on the day of his death, he made two calls to Bob Geldof, engaging in a loud, 20-minute argument. He attempted to persuade Geldof to lift an injunction against Paula Yates, allowing the children to come to Australia for Christmas, but Geldof refused. Hutchence was heard screaming phrases like, "your children hate you. I'm their father, little man." "Hutchins called Bob Geldoff twice. Michael wanted to persuade Bob to drop the cordon junction against Paula and let the three kids come to Australia for Christmas."

xref.title: Recruitment of Musicians for Band-Aid
xref.body: Bob Geldof initiated the Band-Aid project by reaching out to prominent musicians to create a charity single. His first call was to Midge Ure of Ultravox, followed by Sting of The Police, and Simon Le Bon of Duran Duran. As word spread, other notable artists such as Bono, David Bowie, and Paul Weller of The Jam, enthusiastically joined the effort, forming a supergroup of British talent. "First, he called mid-Jour of the band UltraVox. Sting of the police was called next, and Simon LeBawn of Durand Iran, and as words spread more people jumped on board."

xref.title: Sting's Tantric Sex Marathon Myth
xref.body: The widespread story that Sting engages in marathon sessions of tantric sex lasting for hours is completely false. This myth originated from a 1993 "Q Magazine" interview where a drunken Sting, prompted by Sir Bob Geldof, jokingly exaggerated his yoga practice, claiming it allowed him to "retain it all and go on for longer." Sting found the story hysterical and further modified it for fun, leading to the "eight hours at a time" detail, but it was all a lie. "I can take you to higher levels. Yeah, I started to use it to have sex. Now where you don't spill your seed, you retain it all and go on for longer and you never lose control and you just keep going."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
